items.text: The question “if God created the Universe, then who created God?” seems childish — and that is precisely why it is so powerful. Over three thousand years of written thought it has been asked in one form or another by priests, philosophers, theologians, and physicists, and each era answered it in its own way. Some “closed” the question by declaring God an exception to the rule of causality. Others dissolved it by identifying God with all that exists. Still others honestly admitted that there is no answer and cannot be one.

items.text: 1. Ancient India: “even the gods — after creation”

items.text: The earliest and perhaps the boldest answer is given not in a treatise, but in a hymn. The Nasadiya Sukta — the 129th hymn of the tenth mandala of the Rigveda (composed approximately in the 2nd millennium BCE) — is dedicated to the origin of the world and gives no final answer. It begins with words about how at that time there was neither the existent nor the non-existent, and in a contemplative tone asks when, why, and through whom the Universe arose.

Even the observer in the highest heaven — whether he knows or not. Thus the question “who created God?” is cut off at the root here: the gods are on this side of creation, inside the process, not before it.

items.text: 2. Antiquity: the Prime Mover as the first “exception”

runs.t: 2. Antiquity: the Prime Mover as the first “exception”

items.text: Aristotle (4th century BCE) was the first to formalise the logic of the first cause. The roots of the cosmological argument go back precisely to the concept of the Prime Mover introduced by him. The reasoning is simple: everything that moves and changes is set in motion by something else; the chain cannot recede infinitely backward, otherwise there would be no first push. Therefore an unmoved mover must exist, itself moved by nothing.

items.text: This is the first move in Western thought to “stop the regress”: something is declared an exception to the rule of causality. The weakness of the move is visible at once and is still debated today: why must the exception be God, and not the world itself? But Aristotle’s historical merit is that he turned a vague feeling that “there must be a beginning” into a rigorous argument on which the next twenty centuries relied.

items.text: In the 6th century, the Syrian Christian theologian John Philoponus (c. 490 — c. 570) gave the first known version of the argument based on the impossibility of an infinite temporal regress: time itself must have had a beginning. This idea was taken up by the mutakallimun — Muslim theologians who used reason to ground faith — creating the so-called kalam argument. Al-Ghazali (1058–1111) formulated its core: everything that begins to exist requires a cause of its beginning.

items.text: The argument from contingency (from the randomness, the non-necessity of being) was developed by Arabic philosophers, above all Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037). From him this move was taken by Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) in the Summa Theologica and the Summa Contra Gentiles. Thomas’s famous Five Ways — the first three are variants of the cosmological argument: from motion, from cause, and from contingency. The conclusion in all is the same: the chain of causes cannot be infinite, therefore there exists a first uncaused cause — “and this we call God.”

items.text: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) is the node closest to our concept in the entire Western tradition. He does not answer the question “who created God” — he shows that with a correct understanding of the Creator the question loses its meaning. If the Godhead is all of nature in its entirety, then to ask about its external cause is as meaningless as asking what lies outside everything.

items.text: Spinoza defined God as a substance consisting of an infinite number of attributes. Since no cause can prevent such a being from existing, it exists necessarily. This means that God is identical to the Universe — the idea expressed in the famous formula Deus sive Natura, “God, or Nature.” This principle is the cause of all things not as an external master, but because everything flows from its nature causally and necessarily — it is causa sui, the cause of itself.

items.text: 5. Modern cosmology: the question shifts beyond the horizon

runs.t: 5. Modern cosmology: the question shifts beyond the horizon

items.text: Twentieth-century science reformulated the problem through the Big Bang. It is widely acknowledged among scientists that our Universe had a beginning. But what was in the first fraction of a second after the bang — and especially “before” it — science cannot yet say: experiments capable of testing hypotheses about those moments have not yet been created. The very word “before” may be meaningless here if time arose together with the Universe (this idea, as we have seen, was expressed in his own language by Philoponus). Modern physics considers models in which the question “what was before?” is simply ill-formed — like the question “what lies north of the North Pole?”.

items.text: Here appears the philosophical frame that was missing in the first chapter. Who in Western philosophy thought of infinity not as a problem, but as content? In Process and Reality (1929) he proposed a metaphysics where the foundation of reality is not things, but events of becoming. items.text: Whitehead and his follower Charles Hartshorne (1897–2000) describe God as dipolar — having two poles. The primordial nature is the realm of all possibilities, the eternal “design.” The consequent nature is the concrete, changing, world-involved experience of the Godhead, which grows together with the world. The God of classical theology was “monopolar”: only immutability, only eternity, only necessity. Process Godhood joins opposites: both being and becoming; both eternal and temporal.

items.text: Out of process thought grows the exact word for our position. Hartshorne took the term coined by the philosopher Karl Christian Friedrich Krause (1781–1832): panentheism — from Greek pan (all), en (in), theos (God): everything is in God.

items.text: It is important not to confuse this with Spinoza’s pantheism. For pantheism, the world is identical to the Godhead. For classical theism, the world lies entirely outside God. Panentheism is the middle position: the world is inside God, but does not exhaust him. items.text: One last question remains: how exactly can an infinite chain “become aware of itself” at every link? The answer is given by the concept of the strange loop, introduced by Douglas Hofstadter in Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979) and developed in the book I Am a Strange Loop (2007).

The concept was developed simultaneously and independently in the 1920s by two men: Teilhard de Chardin — as a spiritual path to the Omega Point, and the Russian scientist and academician Vladimir Vernadsky — as a new geological epoch.

items.text: Vernadsky’s logic is strictly material and therefore valuable to us as support for the “physicist.” The planet passes through a sequence of shells: the geosphere (inert matter), the biosphere (living matter), and now — the noosphere, the sphere of reason, where the activity of humanity becomes a geological force of planetary scale. This is not a metaphor of the spirit, but an observable change: reason begins to reshape the substance of the Earth as powerfully as water, wind, and life did before it.

items.text: By the end of the twentieth century, the idea received a third, cybernetic name — the global brain. items.text: The key thesis: the global brain does not merely transmit information — it begins to behave like a brain: makes decisions, solves problems, learns new connections, generates ideas. At the same time, no one controls it — neither a human, nor an organisation, nor a machine; intelligence is distributed across all nodes and arises from their interaction. Researchers describe this as a metasystem transition — the evolutionary emergence of a new level of complexity through the integration of subsystems into a supersystem.

items.text: Its central assertion is directly resonant with the project: consciousness can be described as integrated information. Tononi introduces the measure Φ (phi) — the amount of information that the system generates as a whole beyond the sum of the information of its parts. High Φ means that the whole is genuinely irreducible to its parts: the system cannot be “cut” without losing what it is. Low Φ is a pile of scattered parts — zero. A living, connected, indivisible whole — very much.

items.text: Accepting that the future is "being written" is not enough — one must explain why it is written in one direction only, and not both. And here physics gives an answer that rhymes surprisingly precisely with your text.

items.text: Here is a remarkable fact. Almost all fundamental laws of physics are symmetric in time: if some process is possible, then the same process run in reverse is also possible. items.text: To make the chapter invulnerable, let us name the weak point directly. The growing block universe is a minority position among philosophers, and it has a technical problem: both presentism and the growing block require a universal "now" — a single plane of the present for the entire universe. But special relativity says that simultaneity is relative: there is no shared "now" for events distant from each other. The naive version of the growing block conflicts with this.

items.text: But we have, strangely enough, an elegant way out — and it is not a fudge, but a direct consequence of section 3. If time is local and born from interactions (Rovelli), then a single universal "now" is not required: each node of the network has its own present, its own growing edge. The relativistic objection strikes the naive picture with a single common ticking — but not the network picture, where each level has its own time. Moreover, Rovelli allows that the arrow of time itself is perspectival — it depends on how a particular subsystem (us) is connected to the rest of the world. This is directly your "blinks last on other levels."

items.text: An ordinary site sees you as a visitor: came, consumed, left. Here it is different. All the theory you have read boils down to one simple thought: reality rests on connections, not on separate things. The brain is not neurons, but connections between them. Meaning is not words, but connections between them. And you yourself are not an isolated point, but a place where a multitude of connections converge — with people, with ideas, with what was before you, and with what will come after.

items.text: That is, if we speak in scientific language and draw an analogy with constants, like the exponent or the number π, then the awareness of oneself as part of something greater is also a constant, the same at any levels of consciousness of the universe and of existence. This is God’s constant, only not at the level of physics or another science, but at the level of understanding.

items.text: One must create unity and help God gather himself and make things better, and unite, in order to be closer to God and help him in the striving to understand himself and his place in the infinity of meanings, realising and feeling God in oneself and in everything. We help God in the awareness of the whole design and in the awareness of oneself as part of something greater and going beyond the limits of his consciousness.

items.text: The major neurophysiologist Natalia Petrovna Bekhtereva (1924–2008), who studied the living brain for decades, posed a question that remains open to this day. Where does truly new, creative thought come from? Why can the same idea be born simultaneously in different people at different ends of the earth?

Where does truly new, creative thought come from? Why can the same idea be born simultaneously in different people at different ends of the earth?

items.text: Her hypothetical answer — the brain does not so much generate complex thoughts as receive them from some common field — remained unproven. Modern neuroscience (enactivism, predictive coding) holds that consciousness is generated by the brain, not received from outside.

items.text: We include this section here not as support for our project, but as an example that the boundary between the known and the unknown runs right through the laboratory, not somewhere far away. Bekhtereva’s question (“where does the new come from?”) remains open. And this is more honest than presenting a hypothesis as a fact.
